subChunks.title: Singleton & Factory

storyBeats.text: Eldrin explains the Academy Registry — only one exists, consulted by every department. To have two would cause conflicting records and chaos.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Singleton is the simplest pattern — and the most abused. Use it only when you genuinely need exactly one instance: configuration, connection pools, logging systems. Used carelessly, it becomes a global variable and a testing nightmare.

storyBeats.label: Factory pattern

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Factory decouples creation from use. The caller says 'give me a Spell' and doesn't care whether it's fire or ice — the factory decides. This makes adding new spell types trivial: add a new case to the factory, no changes elsewhere.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a SpellFactory that creates spells by type. Support "fire" (prints "Fireball cast!") and "ice" (prints "Ice Lance cast!"). Create one of each and call cast().
guidedPractice.hint: Use a switch expression or ternary in the factory's create() method.

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What problem does the Factory Method pattern solve? How does it enable the Open/Closed principle?

questions.prompt: What is the safest way to implement a Singleton in Java?
options: As an enum with INSTANCE constant
With a private constructor and static field
questions.answer: As an enum with INSTANCE constant
questions.explanation: Enum singletons are inherently thread-safe, serialisation-safe, and immune to reflection-based attacks. They are the preferred Singleton implementation in modern Java (Josh Bloch, Effective Java).

subChunks.title: Builder & Prototype Patterns

storyBeats.text: Eldrin assembles a complex potion — but the constructor has 8 arguments and he keeps forgetting which is which. He redesigns it as a builder.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: The Builder pattern replaces a telescope of constructors with a fluent, self-documenting API. Each method sets one field and returns the builder — enabling method chaining. The final build() constructs the immutable result.

storyBeats.label: Builder in action

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Prototype is builder's cousin — instead of constructing from scratch, you clone an existing object. Expensive initialisation (loading configs, establishing connections) happens once; clones copy the result. The key risk: deep vs shallow copy — ensure mutable fields are properly cloned.

guidedPractice.problemHtml: Implement a Potion.Builder with fields name (String) and power (int). Build a potion with name "Health Elixir" and power 75 and print both fields.
guidedPractice.hint: Each setter in Builder returns 'this'. The build() method calls new Potion(this).

subChunks.feynmanPrompt: What problem does the Builder pattern solve? How does method chaining make it more readable than a constructor with many parameters?

questions.explanation: Each method appends to x and returns this (the builder), enabling chaining. Final value of x is "Hello World".
